chunks: How to spec a brushed motor. The question: How do you spec a motor?
Choosing a motor means starting with the job, not the motor. First work out how much twisting force (torque) and how much speed the load needs.
Then pick a motor, and usually a gearbox, that delivers that with some safety margin.
Finally, check that the supply and the driver (the circuit that switches the motor's power) can handle the current.
It is like picking a vehicle for moving house. First you decide what you must carry and how far. Only then do you choose a van or a truck.
A sports car is fast but cannot carry a sofa. A motor works the same way: a high-speed motor is a poor match for a slow, heavy load unless a gearbox sits between them.
The analogy has one gap: motors also get hot, so how long you run them matters.
Spec flow. Iterate on the gear ratio and winding until all four motor checks pass, then size the electronics and verify on the bench.
Torque: the twisting force at the shaft, in newton-meters (N·m): force in newtons (N) times the lever arm in meters. Gear ratio ( N ): how many motor turns make one output turn.
It trades speed for torque. Duty cycle: the fraction of time the motor is actually running. Stall current: the current with the shaft held still, V over R .
Margin: extra capacity beyond the calculated need, for battery sag and heating.
A robot wheel has a 0. 05 m radius and must push with 2 N. The torque at the wheel is 2 times 0. 05 = 0. 1 N·m .
The wheel should turn at 20 rad/s (radians per second; one turn is about 6. 28 radians).
Suppose the chosen motor runs best near 400 rad/s, so pick a gear ratio of 400 / 20 = 20:1 . The motor then supplies 0. 1 / 20 = 0. 005 N·m. With K t equals 0.
02 N·m/A, that is 0. 005 / 0. 02 = 0. 25 amps . That is the whole idea: work from the load back to the motor.
"I work from the load backwards. Get the output torque and speed, continuous and peak, plus duty cycle, supply voltage, size and life.
Pick a gear ratio that sets motor torque as load torque over N and motor speed as N times load speed.
Then check the motor: continuous torque under its rated continuous value, peak under stall, and enough voltage for back-EMF plus IR with margin.
Current is torque over K t , which sizes the driver, and stall current is V over R . Then check thermal, brush life, noise, mounting and cost, and verify on the bench."
